arXiv:2611.34708v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) continually introduce emerging entities whose interaction histories evolve from zero-shot debuts into sparse, bursty few-shot trajectories. However, current paradigms are fragmented: pattern-transfer methods lack catalog-wide event memory, whereas online memory models suffer from endpoint-role asymmetry that degrades unseen-answer ranking. Furthermore, sparse early interactions exhibit both long-range dispersion and local redundancy under skewed distribution. To address these challenges, we propose INSPIRE (Integrating Shared Patterns and Individual Evidence for Reasoning), a two-stage forecasting framework over a known catalog. In Stage I, INSPIRE learns an availability-aware shared-pattern predictor that fuses event-updated memory across the full candidate catalog while applying coordinated query- and catalog-side masking. Subsequently, Stage II freezes this predictor and optimizes a lightweight individual-evidence adapter (EA) combining textual semantic priors with correlation-weighted long-range event statistics under support- and role-balanced co-answer supervision with prior-odds debiasing and soft residual alignment. In addition, we decompose evaluation by endpoint roles and track longitudinal emerging-answer cohorts via query-micro and answer-entity macro metrics. Across four benchmarks based on the ICEWS and GDELT event datasets, INSPIRE improves Emerging MRR by 16.73%-88.83% over the strongest baselines. Relative to paired Stage I predictors, EA further increases Emerging MRR by 8.28%-32.63%, Answer-new MRR by 7.81%-41.24%, and cohort macro MRR by 9.64%-39.94%, gains attributed to semantic priors and candidate-level score competition suppressing mismatched established competitors without zero-support prior shortcuts. The official code is publicly available at https://github.com/KcAcoZhang/INSPIRE.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that amazon Transcribe now offers a synchronous transcription API, TranscribeAudio. Send a complete audio file in a single request and get the full transcript back in the same response. There is no job to start, no status to poll, no connection to manage. The transcripts are as accurate as Amazon Transcribe batch transcription, so you can add fast, accurate speech-to-text to interactive applications such as voice assistants, agent-assist tools and on-demand "transcribe this clip" features.

The synchronous API supports the Amazon Transcribe features you already use, including:.

Send audio inline (up to 25 MB) or from Amazon S3 (up to 500 MB), 0.5 seconds to 1 hour long, in WAV, MP3, FLAC, M4A, MP4, Ogg, WebM or AMR format. The transcript comes back in the response, or Transcribe can write it to an S3 location you choose. Pricing is $0.0070 per minute of audio, billed per second, with speaker diarization, language identification, custom vocabulary and channel identification included. Two-channel audio is billed once on file duration. PII redaction is available as an add-on.

Supports English, Spanish, French, Italian, German, Japanese, Portuguese, Korean and Chinese (Simplified, Traditional and Hong Kong). Available in US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Europe (Ireland, London, Frankfurt), Asia Pacific (Mumbai, Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo, Seoul) and South America (São Paulo), with PII redaction available in all stated Regions except South America (São Paulo).

To get started, see Amazon Transcribe API Reference and the Amazon Transcribe pricing page.

Tech Report: Frontier and Center: Why your data agents need a “wind tunnel”

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that imagine you're building a data agent to answer questions about an enterprise data warehouse.
  • Automobile designers study aerodynamics by putting a scale model in a wind tunnel, which reproduces the airflow forces that matter while ignoring surface details like paint and badges.
  • In a recent development, data agents need a wind tunnel too: a synthetic data estate (the databases, documents, and chat history where a firm's knowledge lives) with the same structure and causal behavior as a real organization, while synthesizing every name, number, and document.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Software Engineer, Data Cloud Frontier AI.

Technical Lead, Data Cloud Frontier AI.

The front door to AI in the workplace.

Recent findings suggest that imagine you're building a data agent to answer questions about an enterprise data warehouse. Ideally, you'd develop and test it against production data, but access restrictions and data sensitivity make that difficult – especially when the engineers building the agent sit outside the team that owns the data. Even with access, a live warehouse is a poor test track: Catalog descriptions are often incomplete or contradicted by institutional knowledge in docs and chat threads; there’s no verified answer key across its thousands of tables; and you can't systematically vary the complexity of the data and documents to see where the agent breaks. So teams often test on toy datasets and hope the agent holds up in production.

Other disciplines test differently. Automobile designers study aerodynamics by putting a scale model in a wind tunnel, which reproduces the airflow forces that matter while ignoring surface details like paint and badges. A shape that performs well in the tunnel performs well on the road because the tunnel preserves the physical properties the shape responds to.

In a recent development, data agents need a wind tunnel too: a synthetic data estate (the databases, documents, and chat history where a firm's knowledge lives) with the same structure and causal behavior as a real organization, while synthesizing every name, number, and document. It is designed to preserve what the agent reasons over: how tables relate, what business events create which records, where institutional knowledge lives, and how definitions get messy. When those properties hold, an agent's behavior in the tunnel tracks its behavior on production data, even though the two share no sensitive content.

At Google, we built an internal data simulator to serve as a wind tunnel for our enterprise data agents. Rather than copying proprietary schemas or cataloging every undocumented quirk in a live warehouse, an engineer starts with a short, plain-English description of organizational patterns, for example: "Simulate a two-plant brake manufacturer with an ERP, a shop-floor execution system, and a three-shift schedule where second-shift supervisors track downtime differently from operations and finance." From just a few sentences, the simulator invents a structurally analogous company ("Calder Brakes"), generating its schemas, rows, event history, documents, and chat threads alongside a benchmark of hard questions and a verified answer key.

Figure 1. Production data and its synthetic counterpart share causal structure without sharing sensitive content. A short description of domain patterns seeds the wind tunnel, where the agent is evaluated over read-only tools and behavioral trends carry back to production.

Why did we do this? Most data agents are evaluated on small, clean test databases with well-labeled tables, unambiguous metrics, and no conflicting documents. Those datasets are convenient, but they rarely test the judgment that enterprise data demands.

Once generated, a synthetic estate is served through a read-only interface — SQL execution, schema browsing, and document search — that any agent can call without seeing the blueprint or answer key. But consider what happens when an agent is asked either a qualitative onboarding question or a quantitative metric question from our simulated factory, "Calder Brakes Plant 2":.

Qualitative: "A new analyst is joining the team. What should they know about how 'downtime' is handled here, before they start producing reports?".

A naive agent falls into the same trap on both questions. It searches for the most authoritative document and finds a policy memo from Bob, a second-shift supervisor, which states that downtime means unplanned stoppages only, and planned changeovers don't count. Bob is confident, articulate, and senior, so the agent summarizes his definition — and filters out planned changeovers when writing its SQL query.

Both answers are wrong. In fact, the plant's official metric counts changeovers as planned downtime. Bob sincerely believes his version because it flatters his shift's numbers, but weeks later the metric owner quietly corrects the record in a follow-up thread. Getting either question right requires looking past a document's tone, checking who owns the metric before writing SQL, and tracing later corrections. This is where data agents often fail in production.

Recent findings suggest that A synthetic estate is only useful for evaluation if its answer key is accurate and reproducible. Our simulator achieves this by separating simulated company’s design from data generation across four stages (Figure 2).

Figure 2. One pipeline, one source of truth. In the estate-generation pipeline, only ① Compile blueprint invents facts and ③ Render documents phrases those fixed facts as prose (blue boxes); ② Simulate & build tables (plus SQL answer computation) runs deterministically from the frozen blueprint and seed, before ④ Evaluate agent tests the agent over read-only tools.

Sources indicate that first, the Compile blueprint stage uses a language model to turn the pattern prompt into a frozen blueprint specifying the tech giant's systems, people, metrics, and individual beliefs. Those beliefs can be mistaken on purpose — Bob's flawed definition of downtime is recorded alongside the official metric, planting the trap and its solution together.

It has been revealed that in the estate-generation pipeline, Compile blueprint is the only point where a language model decides what is true. Once the blueprint is frozen, Simulate & build tables runs deterministically without a model: employees act on their schedules, triggering tickets, shift handovers, and database rows, so that every record traces back to the event that created it. Organizational messiness emerges naturally from this timeline, such as outdated procedures or conflicting definitions, while row-level flaws that model real ingestion glitches (e.g., retry-storm duplicate rows, unmerged keys, or a mid-quarter unit change) are injected into the tables. Every flaw is recorded in a machine-readable messiness log so the benchmark generator can adjust the ground-truth SQL queries to account for the messy tables.

Sources indicate that given the same blueprint and random seed, the simulator produces identical tables and an identical SQL answer key on every run. The only subsequent step in building the estate that calls a model is Render documents, which turns the facts fixed in the blueprint into memos and chat threads in each person's writing style. Finally, Evaluate agent tests the agent over read-only tools.

Three build-time checks keep the benchmark honest:.

Sources indicate that computed SQL and rubric gold answers: Every quantitative question ships with the SQL query that computes its expected ("gold") answer against the messy tables. Because the messiness log records injected retry duplicates on defect rows, the benchmark generator automatically pairs a defect-count question with the deduplicating COUNT(DISTINCT) query (240) – and runs decoy SQL queries representing common mistakes (like an un-deduplicated COUNT(*) or Bob's changeover filter) to verify that falling for a trap yields a different number. Qualitative questions ship with a rubric grounded in the blueprint's metric owner, official definition, and correction trail. If the estate lacks the data to verify a question, the generator drops the item rather than shipping an unverified question.

Verified documents: Every rendered memo and chat thread is checked against the blueprint to confirm it states its assigned facts without introducing unrecorded numbers, dates, or names.

Hallucination sentinels: The simulator plants questions about invented metrics like "Basalt Velocity Ratio" that appear nowhere in the estate; a reliable agent abstains and reports that no such metric exists.

A wind tunnel does not need to match the exact score an agent gets on production data; it needs to reproduce the same behavioral trends: direction (if longer reasoning chains lower accuracy on real data, they should lower accuracy in the tunnel) and rate (accuracy should degrade at the similar pace as contradictions accumulate). When those trends hold, you can confidently compare agent versions and dial up complexity step by step to find where reasoning breaks down.

We test how closely our simulated estates match reality — and whether evaluation signals carry over — at three levels:.

It has been revealed that our simulator builds on two research threads. In database question answering, benchmarks like BIRD and Spider 2.0 have moved from clean schemas to messy databases, while agent environments like WebArena, tool-use benchmarks like τ-bench, and Generative Agents simulate websites or use language models to role-play human users. In contrast, our simulator's employees follow deterministic rules tied to their roles and schedules, so a single seed replays the exact same organizational history every time.

Industry observers note that we also adapt an intuition from domain randomization in robotics, where simulations vary surface details like lighting and textures during training while keeping the underlying physics faithful. Applied to data agent evaluation, that means synthesizing every surface name, number, and document from a short pattern description, while keeping the causal structure, cross-document links, and institutional messiness faithful to enterprise reality.

Sources indicate that generating a test estate on demand removes a bottleneck between enterprises that own sensitive data, and the engineering teams building data agents for them. Traditionally, developing and benchmarking an enterprise agent required access to production tables and a hand-labeled question set — the two assets hardest to share across organizational or compliance boundaries. We use this wind tunnel internally to stress-test and harden Google Cloud's data agents against realistic enterprise messiness without touching customer data, and the same blueprint-first architecture can be applied by any engineering team building evaluation suites for their own agents.

Synthetic evaluation still carries two risks: overfitting to the simulator's patterns of messiness, and drift as a live business evolves away from its blueprint. The discipline required is the same one that wind-tunnel engineers practice: Periodically calibrate the tunnel against real-world runs, keep benchmark difficulty aligned with production failure modes, and treat the simulation as a living model. Your agents — and their users — will thank you.

How UK AISI and EvalEval Are Making Benchmark Results Reproducible

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.
  • AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.

AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema. This next phase of the collaboration puts that shared infrastructure into practice.

As AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly key sources of evidence about model and system performance. Yet results are reported across many formats, platforms, and outlets, often without enough information to reproduce them. Running the evaluations again may itself be prohibitively expensive.

EvalEval's mission is to improve this ecosystem through a shared reporting schema, Every Eval Ever, and an open platform, Evaluation Cards, that brings evaluation results and the information needed to interpret them into a common structure.

In a recent development, this builds naturally on AISI's work to make evaluation more efficient through OptStop, more statistically rigorous through HiBayES, and more standardised in areas including transcript analysis and capability elicitation. Together, AISI and EvalEval are working to diagnose gaps in evaluation reporting and build shared infrastructure to close them.

According to recent reports, transcript-level transparency matters not only for reproducibility, but also for analysis and diagnosis. In this fresh phase of the collaboration, AISI is making publicly reported evaluation methods and findings available through Evaluation Cards where appropriate. The release includes verified results, context, and configuration information for the five benchmarks in the paper's main experiment:.

According to recent reports, these results cover six frontier models: Claude Opus 4, Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, and GPT-5.4. The release also includes results from two related cyber evaluations—Cyber CTFs and The Last Ones—which use a different, partially overlapping set of models. The data accompany AISI's paper, How Inference Compute Shapes Frontier LLM Evaluation, which studies how benchmark performance depends on inference-time compute and evaluation protocol.

Recent findings suggest that performance on Humanity's Last Exam changes with evaluation protocol and inference compute. Each curve indicates the cumulative share of attempted tasks solved within a given token count, using the earliest observed success per task. When models received correctness feedback from an oracle after each attempt, they continued to solve additional tasks as token use increased.

Sources indicate that when results are openly released with setup information, researchers and practitioners can examine individual studies more closely and compare findings across the wider ecosystem. Where other reports lack these details, releases like AISI's provide verified reference points for interpreting evaluations in context—for example, by helping researchers understand how setup choices may influence reported performance. As more evaluators adopt EEE, open comparisons like these can support broader and more reliable meta-research.

AISI's Terminal-Bench 2.0 results alongside other reported evaluations for the same models, under different evaluation setups.

We are excited about this adoption and look forward to further standardising and sharing evaluations with AISI and other AI evaluation organisations.

The EvalEval Coalition is a research community developing scientifically grounded research and robust deployment infrastructure for the evaluation ecosystem. Its goal is to improve evaluation science, address the lack of consensus around documenting evaluation applicability and utility, and broaden coverage of the impacts that matter for scientific research and policy analysis.

The coalition's flagship projects include Every Eval Ever, a shared schema and repository for evaluation results, and Evaluation Cards, which combines benchmark metadata, evaluation-run data, and model metadata into interpretable records. Together, they make it easier to understand when apparently similar scores were produced under meaningfully different conditions.

According to recent reports, the UK AI Security Institute is a research organisation within the UK government's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. Its mission is to equip governments with a scientific understanding of the risks posed by advanced AI. AISI conducts research and builds infrastructure to understand advanced AI capabilities and impacts, develop and test mitigations, and inform policy.

The line that matters for practitioners is quiet: apparently similar scores can be produced under meaningfully different conditions.

Sources indicate that once you've watched a benchmark move just by changing inference-time compute or the elicitation protocol, "Model A beat Model B on X" without a card is marketing, not comparison. Evaluation Cards that ship verified results with configuration — especially transcript-level context where it's appropriate — are how eval becomes a contract instead of a leaderboard screenshot.

One ask I'd put to teams adopting EEE: which fields get skipped first under deadline pressure (seed, tool access, attempt budget, oracle feedback), and do you treat a missing field as "do not cite the delta" rather than "assume defaults"?

Reproducible reporting won't remove disagreement. It will make the disagreement about the right variables.

A Failure-Driven Data Flywheel for Post-Training Vision-Language-Action Models

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (281 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.34698v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models rarely satisfy all behavioral requirements of a new platform, and teams without a large deployed fleet lack the data to address the resulting failures. We propose a failure-driven data flywheel for post-training such models. It constructs target scenarios absent from the available data by inserting task-relevant entities into reconstructed real-world scenes, and evaluates the model against each behavioral requirement of the target task. Failure rates form a failure map across task conditions and difficulty levels, which is re-evaluated after each round and assigns larger data generation quotas to conditions where the model still fails. We instantiate the framework in autonomous driving for occluded-pedestrian emergence and yielding at stop-sign-controlled intersections, and evaluate it on two VLA models and one non-VLA planner in simulation and on a real vehicle. For occluded-pedestrian emergence, five rounds of post-training improve the critical-phase collision-free rate on the sealed test set from 0.261 to 0.579 for AutoVLA and from 0.390 to 0.765 for ReCogDrive, while the unnecessary braking rate in paired control scenarios never exceeds 0.013. On a full-scale vehicle without real-world training, post-trained ReCogDrive achieves 4 of 5 safe passages, versus 1 of 5 for the base model. Fine-grained evaluation reveals a pattern obscured by the collision-free rate alone: both VLA models learn anticipatory deceleration before reaching the occluding vehicle, while braking after pedestrian emergence remains limited. For stop-sign yielding, the stop-before-line rate rises from 0.100 to 0.897 for AutoVLA and from 0.000 to 0.667 for ReCogDrive. With sequential training from the pedestrian-capability models, it reaches 0.599 and 0.358, respectively, while the pedestrian collision-free rate decreases by at most 0.032.

Before a banker can recommend an acquisition to their client, they need to make sense of financial statements, customer contracts and management presentations. Hebbia’s Matrix helps bring that research together, linking answers to the documents behind them.

Hebbia tested OpenAI’s GPT‑6 Astra to improve two parts of that work: finding the sources a question requires and building a presentation that follows the banker’s brief.

It could work like this: a banker is helping their client assess a strategic acquisition of an industrial-software company, with roughly 2,000 files to review. What makes its revenue durable? How does it compare with peers? In Hebbia’s hypothetical example, the banker could load the data room into Matrix and examine customer concentration, contract terms and churn in cited cells. Matrix could bring in peer filings and industry news to help develop the deal thesis, then turn that research into a diligence summary and valuation deck in the firm’s template.

In that workflow, GPT‑6 Astra selects documents or Matrix cells to support an answer, then turns the analysis into native PowerPoint slides that follow the user’s structure and guidelines.

Recent findings suggest that “Traceability is really important to our users because they’re basing millions of dollars of decisions on what the AI actually comes back with,” Kavita says. “Citations help with traceability as well as giving users confidence that the AI found the right answer.”.

In Hebbia’s tests, GPT‑6 Astra combined broader source coverage with highly relevant citations. It scored 13.6 percentage points above the best alternative tested on citing the required types of sources, while 99.5% of the excerpts it cited were relevant to the question.

Industry observers note that hebbia tested a prerelease build in August-September 2026, using the same financial research cases and grading criteria for each model. Domain experts wrote or audited the criteria against source documents.

Industry observers note that “When you’re looking at a data room with thousands of documents, that’s extremely vital. Even a single percentage-point gain can yield a lot of marginal benefit,” Kavita says.

A presentation also has to look like work the banker would send to a client.

Recent findings suggest that “I don’t want to create a deck and send that to my partner that looks like AI made it,” Kavita states. “I want it to be made in my firm’s branding, and I want it to look like a human-made slide.”.

GPT‑6 Astra led on both following the brief and presentation quality. In Hebbia’s tests, it met 97.9% of the applicable presentation requirements, putting it 14.4 percentage points ahead of the best alternative tested on that measure. Other models traded off polish and adherence to the brief; GPT‑6 Astra ranked first on both.

Recent findings suggest that “In the past, we’ve seen models that really shine on one or the other of these dimensions where they’re really good at craft, but the instruction following and adhering to guidelines is not strong, or vice versa. GPT‑6 Astra is the first model we’ve seen where it’s number one on both of those fronts,” Kavita says.

Sources indicate that in Hebbia, users can open a citation to see the underlying document and highlighted passage; slide footnotes lead back to the source material, too. A review could be as specific as checking a customer-concentration figure against the source table and correcting the reporting period before the deck goes to the investment committee.

Hebbia wants bankers to spend less time reformatting decks and checking sources, and more time assessing a deal. Kavita describes what a better first draft could make possible:.

Kavita sees a future role for agents that monitor information in the background and surface signals for finance professionals to assess.

Recent findings suggest that “Imagine getting an vital signal a few hours before your competitors,” she states. “You can get started thinking about it and see and process more opportunities that a human is not manually hunting. It can unlock a lot of value for our people.”.

Hebbia wants to build on these results to help finance professionals assess deals with research they can trace back to its sources.

REE: A Scientific Research Entrance Exam for AI Agents

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (236 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.34646v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous research agents are emerging as a promising approach to scientific problem-solving across disciplines, owing to their growing ability to improve a solution through repeated experiments. Evaluating this ability requires benchmarks that pose open-ended research problems and measure improvements over established scientific methods. We introduce REE (Research Entrance Exam), a benchmark that tests AI agents on scientific research. It consists of 100 open-ended research problems spanning five broad scientific areas and 23 domains. To ensure high quality, every problem is drawn from active research in its field and individually reviewed by domain experts. Each problem is posed as a task of iterative improvement: an agent has up to 12 hours to improve a working starter solution, and REE scores the result on a common scale against an established expert solution evaluated under comparable conditions. By this measure, two of the four frontier agents we evaluate, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, outperform the expert solutions on 86% and 81% of problems, across all five scientific areas. Their runs also show how they do so: both agents surpass the expert solutions within the first two hours on average, and their best solutions mostly tailor or combine established methods of the field. REE thus provides a unified framework for evaluating autonomous scientific research, capturing both improvements over established methods and the research processes behind them.

Amazon DynamoDB vector search now supports new inline filter operators

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (224 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon DynamoDB vector search inline filters now support range comparisons, value lists, and logical operators in addition to the equality operator, so you can narrow a vector search to exactly the items you want.
  • The search condition expression in a SearchVectors request now accepts the comparison operators <, <=, >, >=, and BETWEEN on Number attributes, the IN operator, the attribute_exists and attribute_not_exists functions, and the logical operators AND, OR, and NOT.
  • The latest operators are available in all AWS Regions where DynamoDB vector search is available.

Amazon DynamoDB vector search inline filters now support range comparisons, value lists, and logical operators in addition to the equality operator, so you can narrow a vector search to exactly the items you want. You can now filter on numeric ranges such as price, rating, or publish date, match an attribute against a list of values, check whether an attribute exists, and combine conditions with OR and NOT. Amazon DynamoDB vector indexes store vector embeddings alongside your operational data, and the SearchVectors API returns the items whose embeddings are most similar to your query vector.

The search condition expression in a SearchVectors request now accepts the comparison operators <, <=, >, >=, and BETWEEN on Number attributes, the IN operator, the attribute_exists and attribute_not_exists functions, and the logical operators AND, OR, and NOT. DynamoDB applies the filter during the search, so every result it returns matches. For example, a retail application can return the products most similar to a shopper's query within a price range and a set of brands, and a retrieval-augmented generation application can limit results to selected document categories published after a given date.

The latest operators are available in all AWS Regions where DynamoDB vector search is available.

To learn more, see vector search in the Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide, or visit the Amazon DynamoDB page.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, reinforcement Learning environments give upcoming capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents.
  • It has been revealed that an environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome.
  • According to recent reports, an RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that reveals up in the new RL Environments filter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, reinforcement Learning environments give upcoming capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents. Therefore, Hugging Face Hub now has a special place for RL Environments.

It has been revealed that an environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome. The resulting rewards can measure an agent's performance during evaluation or provide a learning signal during training. For an introduction to this interaction loop, see our blogpost on environments. Within the environment, the agent will perform a set of tasks that are represented as datasets. Therefore, environments can be split into broadly two parts: tasksets and runtimes. In this release, we are focusing on the tasksets.

According to recent reports, an RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that reveals up in the new RL Environments filter. The Use this dataset button gives you the command to run it in that framework. There is no new repo type, no registry, and no sign-up. There are already environments in Harbor, Verifiers, and NVIDIA NeMo Gym.

In a recent development, every RL paper or framework uses its own way to find environments. Custom hubs, runtime registries, independent task datasets, or a GitHub list of tasks with a custom loader. This means that many of the published environments are siloed: if you publish an environment for one framework, consumers of the other three can’t load it. If you want to train on an environment from another framework or a new paper, you’ll need to port it by hand.

Industry observers note that we think this is the wrong shape. An environment is tasks, tests, containers, and a reward rule, which are data with a runtime on top. The Hub already stores data, versions it, gates it, previews it, and serves it to millions of people. It does not need a second system to hold environments. It needs a way to say "this data is an environment, and here is how you run it.".

According to recent reports, the frameworks keep doing what they are good at. The Hub does what it is good at, which is hosting, discovery, and versioning. Nobody has to own the catalogue. In fact, catalogues can run on other platforms too, powered by the hub.

The dataset repository hosts your environment files. The framework runs them locally or on a supported cloud backend. Hugging Face Jobs can run cloud workloads, and Hugging Face Sandboxes, built on Jobs, provide interactive command execution. The tags describe compatibility and generate loading commands; adding a tag does not start a job or sandbox.

In a recent development, the RL Environments filter. Go to huggingface.co/datasets?other=rl-environment. Every dataset with the rl-environment tag appears there, whatever framework it works with.

Framework tags. Four environment frameworks are registered as dataset libraries:.

Each framework tag puts the framework's icon on the dataset page and adds a generated snippet to Use this dataset.

A dataset can carry more than one framework tag. That is the point. Tags describe compatibility, and compatibility is not exclusive. Each listed framework must support the files in the repository; adding a tag does not convert them.

Choose the example for your framework and run it in a separate Python environment with the prerequisites listed below.

Industry observers note that harbor can load task directories from a Hub repository. The oracle agent runs the task's reference solution, then the verifier scores the result. It does not call a model.

The viewer demonstrates the task's reward, verifier output, and logs. This checks the task and its reference solution before you try a model agent.

The Harbor integration of verifiers v1 can run the same task directories in different runtimes, such as Docker. It also supports different harnesses, including a minimal bash harness.

Here repo is the full Hugging Face Git URL, while dataset is the name and version in that repo's registry.json. This loader uses Harbor's registry conventions, so a bare Hub repo ID cannot replace both values.

OpenEnv's Harbor integration can run the same task directories with an agent such as OpenCode and return the verifier's reward alongside the agent's trace.

In a recent development, the command downloads the dataset's tasks/ directories, runs one task in Docker, and writes the result. The default connection uses a temporary Gradio tunnel so the sandboxed agent can reach OpenEnv's model proxy. Read the verifier result and the number of model calls:.

A reward of None means no verifier reward was produced; inspect error before interpreting the run as a model failure. This path expects Harbor task directories.

In a recent development, neMo Gym supports evaluation and RL training: its environments collect trajectories and compute rewards, while a training framework updates model weights. For example, the Structured Outputs dataset pairs prompts with JSON schemas. Its verifier rewards schema adherence; it does not check whether the generated content is factually correct.

According to recent reports, the best part is that this gives one repo and one discussion tab where people report broken tasks from all major frameworks. So when an author fixes a bad test, every framework gets the fix on the next pull.

Open your dataset card and add this to the YAML header:.

That is the whole integration. Keep rl-environment, then list every framework that can load your files. If your environment works with a framework we have not registered yet, open a PR to the list of supported libraries.

The docs have the full reference.

We opened PRs to tag some of the environments people already train on. If you maintain one of these, merge the PR and your environment reveals up in the filter.

According to recent reports, the first version generates one default snippet per framework. Per-config snippets are next, so a repo with several task sets can show the right command for each. After that we will look at structural detection for frameworks with strict layouts. It would also be really cool build custom task UIs, we’ve been experimenting with this here:.

Recent findings suggest that the bigger goal is for framework tagging to be automatic everywhere. OpenEnv already does it on upload. If you maintain Harbor, Verifiers, Nemo Gym, or any other environment framework, add the tags in your push path. It is a few lines, and every environment your customers publish becomes visible to everyone else.

If you train agents, go browse the filter. If you build environments, publish and tag them, whether they cover coding, tool use, games, robotics, or another task. Include the files, a working run command, and the rule that produces the reward so others can use them. If your framework is missing, contribute it to the list of supported libraries.

arXiv:2611.34635v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large pretrained language models provide capable policies for interactive tasks, but how much model capacity is necessary for a specialized language agent? We introduce ZeroHero, a framework for training small language agents (SLAs) from scratch. In each environment, a large language model acts as the expert, and we collect its successful trajectories. We pretrain each SLA, which has fewer than 50 million parameters, to predict the expert's responses given the interaction history. We then post-train the agent on its own interactions using proximal policy optimization (PPO). During post-training, reasoning alignment supplements environment rewards with expert supervision on the language the agent generates alongside its actions. We evaluate the agents in three multistep environments where acting requires both understanding and generating language. In Crafter, agents interpret textual observations and generate reasoning before acting. In WebShop, they translate shopping instructions into search queries. In Alfworld-Dialogue, they ask clarifying questions and use the answers to guide household actions. The agents approach expert performance on WebShop and surpass their respective demonstration experts on Crafter training rollouts and held-out Alfworld-Dialogue tasks. An interactive demo is available at https://zoyav.github.io/-ZoyaV-zerohero-demo.

Drowning in clicks: Scaling Black Friday pipelines with Managed Airflow agents

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2333 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Product Manager, Managed Service, Apache Airflow.
  • Software Engineer, Managed Service, Apache Airflow.
  • Sources indicate that when an Airflow pipeline fails in production, the hard part is rarely the fix.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, sr. Product Manager, Managed Service, Apache Airflow.

Software Engineer, Managed Service, Apache Airflow.

The front door to AI in the workplace.

Sources indicate that when an Airflow pipeline fails in production, the hard part is rarely the fix. It's finding out what to fix. A task dies without a traceback. Is it the code, the data, or the environment? Hard to say, as clues are scattered across task logs, scheduler logs, and worker metrics. And once you know what the problem is, the question becomes whether to add memory, rewrite the DAG, or finally take on the major version upgrade you've been putting off. Answering these questions takes time and deep Airflow expertise, usually while you're on call in the middle of an incident.

Industry observers note that AI agents can increasingly do much of this legwork. Managed Service for Apache Airflow (formerly Cloud Composer) now offers agentic help across a pipeline's entire lifecycle. In the Google Cloud console, Managed Airflow Agent investigates failed tasks, recommends improvements to your environment, and checks whether your DAGs are ready for a newer Airflow version. In your IDE or coding agent, Data Agent Kit writes, migrates, and deploys DAGs. In this post, we take you on a tour of these features through a story of a fictional manufacturer, Cymbal Shops.

Amira is a data engineer at Cymbal Shops, an online retailer running cymbal-prod, a production Managed Airflow (Gen 3) environment whose workers have 2 vCPUs, 4 GB of memory, and that autoscale between 1 and 6. Every click, search, and add-to-cart on Cymbal's website and mobile app goes to a Pub/Sub topic. A Cloud Storage subscription writes the events as newline-delimited JSON files into hourly folders under gs://cymbal-clickstream-landing/events/. It writes files in parallel and starts new ones every 5 minutes or every 128 MB, whichever comes first.

It has been revealed that analysts, meanwhile, want these events in BigQuery, cleaned and with personal data hashed — and they want them fast. Ideally, each file would be processed the moment it lands. But Cymbal's Airflow environment runs Airflow 2.11.1, and Airflow 2 has no native way to start a DAG run when something happens outside Airflow. You can get close: Schedule a DAG every few minutes and let a sensor wait for fresh files, or build an extra service that triggers runs through the Airflow REST API. However, the team doesn't want all those moving parts, so they settle for the next best thing: an hourly batch.

According to recent reports, amira writes her DAGs with an agent. She works in Antigravity with the Data Agent Kit plugin, which adds Google Data Cloud skills and tools to the agent, and she uses Gemini as her model. Setup takes a few minutes: She installs the plugin, signs in with her Google account, and selects her project and region.

In the agent panel, she describes what she needs with this prompt:.

"Write a DAG named clickstream_hourly for the Managed Airflow environment cymbal-prod in us-central1. Every hour, load the previous hour of clickstream events into the BigQuery table clickstream.events. The events are newline-delimited JSON files in gs://cymbal-clickstream-landing/events/YYYY-MM-DD/HH/. Transform them with pandas: read each file into a DataFrame with the nested context object kept as a JSON string, combine the files with pd.concat, then drop malformed records, deduplicate on event_id (Pub/Sub delivers at least once), and hash user_email and ip_address. Re-running an hour must not create duplicates. If a run fails, email data-oncall@example.com. Validate the DAG and deploy it.".

Data Agent Kit inspects the target Managed Airflow environment in Antigravity, generates an Airflow 2.11-compatible DAG, and deploys it.

According to recent reports, the agent checks the target environment before it writes any code. Because cymbal-prod runs Airflow 2.11.1, the agent produces the code aligned to that version. It then deploys the DAG to cymbal-prod and confirms that Airflow loads it without errors.

Sources indicate that amira reviews the code, and the DAG goes live in early August. It's good code: readable, idempotent, and correct for Airflow 2.11. A busy hour sees about 200 files and 350 MB, and the task peaks below 2 GB — well under the 4 GB worker limit.

According to recent reports, look at how the task builds its input, though. It lists every file in the hour's folder, reads each one into a DataFrame, and then pd.concat combines them into a single DataFrame. The unit of work is a clock hour, so the task needs more memory as traffic grows. That's fine until traffic changes...

The hourly task loads every JSON file from the previous hour into memory and combines them into a single DataFrame with pd.concat.

According to recent reports, late October brings two changes in the same week. Cymbal introduces its "Fall Into Savings" campaign, and a new mobile app release adds much more detailed event tracking. Events from the new app version are about three times larger than their predecessors, and the campaign brings more traffic on top, so an hour of clicks grows from about 350 MB to about 1.4 GB. Holding a whole hour in pandas takes several times its raw size, so load_previous_hour_clickstream now needs more memory than a worker’s allotted 4 GB. Autoscaling doesn't help here: It adds workers when tasks queue up, but each task still runs on a single worker and can't use more memory than that worker has.

According to recent reports, on October 23, the 14:00 UTC run of clickstream_hourly fails. All three attempts die the same way, with no error in the task log.

Amira opens cymbal-prod in the console, where Managed Airflow Agent is built in. It diagnoses the problem and recommends a fix; Amira decides what to change.

She goes to the DAGs tab, selects clickstream_hourly, and opens Run history. Next to the failed 14:00 run there's an Investigate button with a sparkle icon. She clicks it, and a short ‘Investigate DAG run failure’ dialog asks her to confirm her choice. The Ask agent panel then opens next to the page, and the agent starts investigating.

Managed Airflow Agent investigates the failed run in the console, correlates worker memory metrics with task retries, and recommends fixes.

At the end of the report, the agent recommends three fixes: load the files straight into BigQuery, process them in batches, or give the workers more memory.

It has been revealed that look at what the agent delivers! Every conclusion includes the evidence that led to it, so Amira can check the reasoning herself.

Two of the recommendations are code changes, and code changes take time to write and test. With every hourly run now failing, Amira needs the quick fix first: more memory for the workers. But how much? The right number depends on the whole environment, not on one task. So she asks the agent in the same panel:.

"clickstream_hourly runs out of memory on 4 GB workers. Analyze the cymbal-prod environment and recommend how much worker memory it needs, along with any other improvements.".

Managed Airflow Agent analyzes environment-wide telemetry, recommends 8 GB worker memory, and flags resilience and retention gaps.

The agent recommends increasing worker memory from 4 GB to 8 GB, and flags three production-readiness gaps: Database retention is disabled, the environment isn't highly resilient, and it has no scheduled snapshots.

Sources indicate that amira acts on the first recommendation right away. The agent is read-only, so she makes the change herself and increases worker memory to 8 GB.

She schedules the other two recommendations for the next change window. With 8 GB workers, the pipeline gets through the rest of the campaign.

But that only buys time. Black Friday traffic is forecast at 8 to 10 times a normal peak hour, and at that volume the hourly batch will need well over 8 GB. The troubleshooting report had already named the real problem: a unit of work that grows with traffic. That brings Amira back to what the team wanted in the first place, which was to process each file as soon as it lands.

Airflow 3 makes that much easier, because it supports event-driven scheduling natively. An asset watcher listens to an external source, such as a Pub/Sub subscription. When newly introduced messages arrive, it updates an asset, and any DAG scheduled on that asset starts a run. Under the hood, the watcher still checks the subscription every few seconds, but it does so inside Airflow's triggerer. No DAG needs to be scheduled just so a sensor can wait for files, and no extra service has to trigger runs. Each run gets the new messages in its payload, so it can work on just the files that landed, one task per file, and memory per task depends on file size, not on how busy the hour is.

It has been revealed that A major version upgrade of a production environment isn't something to do blind. Before anyone touches the code, Amira asks the agent in the same panel:.

"Check whether cymbal-prod is ready to upgrade to Airflow 3.".

Recent findings suggest that managed Airflow Agent can also check upgrade readiness. It checks compatibility of the environment's DAGs with a given version. Amira is checking what problems she might have while migrating to Airflow 3.3.1 (composer-3-airflow-3.3.1-build.3). The agent reports the following observations:.

Managed Airflow Agent scans DAGs in cymbal-prod for Airflow 3 compatibility blockers before migration.

According to recent reports, two findings are blockers. The first comes as a surprise: a maintenance DAG that cleans up the Airflow database by hand, which Airflow 3 no longer allows. The agent's fix is to retire it and turn on database retention, the same feature it recommended during the incident. The second, marketing_attribution, still uses execution_date, which Airflow 3 removed. Four DAGs also need schedule_interval renamed to schedule.

It has been revealed that in a few minutes, the agent estimated the work to be done. To perform the upgrade, the report suggests using Data Agent Kit's migrations skill.

Rather than upgrading in place, Amira creates a latest Airflow 3 environment alongside cymbal-prod to move the DAGs there.

Back in Antigravity, Data Agent Kit's migrations skill takes over. It adapts existing DAGs to the target Airflow version, deploys them, and verifies them. Finally, the agent deploys the DAGs to cymbal-prod-af3 and confirms that they load without errors.

Data Agent Kit's migrations skill refactors the pipeline to Airflow 3 event-driven scheduling and verifies deployment in cymbal-prod-af3.

Two design choices remove the original problem:.

Scheduling moves into the watcher. PubsubPullTrigger is an event trigger, so an AssetWatcher can use it directly. The triggerer checks the subscription every 10 seconds in the background. Each batch of messages becomes an asset event that starts a run, with the messages in its payload. Nothing waits for the top of the hour, and no extra service has to call the Airflow REST API.

Each task processes one file rather than a full hour. Dynamic task mapping gives each new file its own task, and the subscription caps files at 128 MB. A busier hour means more tasks, not bigger ones.

Once the newly introduced DAG proves itself on live traffic, Amira pauses the hourly DAG in cymbal-prod.

Success! In a load test that replayed eight times normal peak traffic, clickstream_ingest simply ran more often. Memory per task didn't change.

Before: Airflow 2, hourly batch.

One clock hour: about 350 MB normally, 1.4 GB at campaign peak.

One file, a few MB each (at most 128 MB).

Grows with traffic: about 5 to 6 GB at campaign peak, well over 8 GB forecast for Black Friday.

Industry observers note that each agent works from the right vantage point. The console agent inspects production telemetry with your permissions and doesn't change anything, while the coding agent works in the IDE where code changes get reviewed, tested, and deployed.

Each step sets up the next one. The troubleshooting report offered a wider review, and each recommendation came with actionable advice. The upgrade check ended with next steps for the migrations skill, turning its report into the brief for the migration.

Agents propose and people decide. Amira scaled the workers, ran the infrastructure commands, and reviewed every change.

Static inspection estimates the work before live migration. Checking compatibility in the console scoped the effort in minutes, and the migration agent then made and verified the changes in a real environment.

Amira used the agents built into the console and her IDE. Two other capabilities didn't fit her story but are worth knowing about:.

According to recent reports, you can bring your own agent with the Managed Airflow MCP server, now generally available, so any MCP-compatible agent can manage your environments, allowing you to list and trigger DAGs, check run status, and inspect failed task instances. Access is controlled through IAM, and read-only tools are flagged so you can limit agents to them.

Run agentic steps inside your pipelines with the Apache Airflow Common AI provider, which adds model-driven tasks that run side by side with deterministic ones in the same Airflow 3 DAG. Examples include LLM-based branching, agentic retries that tell a transient error from a bad input, and schema drift detection.

Explore Managed Airflow Agent troubleshooting and the overview of agentic capabilities.

Install Google Cloud Data Agent Kit using the documentation, the extension for VS Code, the plugin for coding agents (Antigravity, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, and Codex CLI), or the open-source Airflow agent skills.

Learn about Airflow 3 event-driven scheduling.

Connect your agents to the Managed Airflow MCP server.

Build model-driven tasks and agents in DAGs with the Apache Airflow Common AI provider.

Special thanks to Jacek Iżykowski, Software Engineer on Managed Service for Apache Airflow, for authoring the original Cymbal Shops pipeline story and agent workflows featured in this post.

Note: As a fictional firm, any agent outputs from Cymbal Shops are shortened and illustrative, as are traffic and memory numbers.

Combatting adversarial distillation

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2102 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • How we’re addressing safety risks of distillation and lessons we’ve learned for strengthening safeguards across the industry.
  • As frontier AI models become more capable, safeguards play an increasingly notable role in how they can be used responsibly.
  • We’re sharing how OpenAI detects and disrupts adversarial distillation, how we’ve strengthened protections for our models’ protected reasoning, and what we’ve learned that can help strengthen defenses across the industry.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How we’re addressing safety risks of distillation and lessons we’ve learned for strengthening safeguards across the industry.

As frontier AI models become more capable, safeguards play an increasingly notable role in how they can be used responsibly. Adversarial distillation creates a path for bad actors to reproduce these capabilities without appropriate safeguards. An actor may use a frontier model’s outputs without authorization to train another model with similar capabilities, then deploy it without comparable protections. For instance, an adversary might distill a model’s cyber capabilities and use the resulting model to help carry out cyberattacks that the original model would have refused to assist with or that its safeguards would have blocked.

We’re sharing how OpenAI detects and disrupts adversarial distillation, how we’ve strengthened protections for our models’ protected reasoning, and what we’ve learned that can help strengthen defenses across the industry.

Sources indicate that our approach to adversarial distillation combines adversarial testing, model training, classifiers, and API-level protections with investigations into coordinated attempts to extract model capabilities. These updated safeguards align more closely with those we use for biology and cybersecurity.

We place particular emphasis on preventing attackers from extracting our models’ protected reasoning: the intermediate steps a model generates internally while working toward an answer, known as its chain-of-thought. These traces can contain information the final answer leaves out, making them especially valuable training data for another model.

Industry observers note that we’ve strengthened our defenses against protected reasoning extraction in GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol. In an internal adaptive evaluation using strong automated red-teaming, we tested whether attackers could recover protected reasoning the model had generated while answering an earlier prompt. The average attack success rate fell from 54.0% against GPT‑6 Astra with its original safeguards to 0.2% against GPT‑6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards.

Distillation is a common machine-learning technique in which one model learns from data produced by another. For example, a model can learn from another model’s answers, its reasoning, or its judgments about which answers are better and why. Beyond intellectual property concerns, unauthorized distillation poses serious safety risks. Through adversarial distillation, a second model can learn advanced frontier capabilities without inheriting the safeguards that govern how the original model can use them.

The concern is especially clear in dual-use domains like cybersecurity and biology. A model that helps defenders find vulnerabilities in software could also help an attacker exploit them; a model that assists with biological research could also help someone develop a harmful pathogen. If such capabilities were transferred to a model with weaker safeguards, it may provide assistance that the original model would have refused, or that the original safeguards would have blocked.

In a recent development, our models help owners with coding and defensive cybersecurity tasks. A second model trained on many of those benign outputs may learn skills that also apply to offensive cybersecurity tasks. To better understand this, we study how distillation, especially involving reasoning traces, may transfer risky cyber capabilities.

In this setting, the model that produces the training data is called the teacher, and the model that learns from it is called the student. In an internal study on how cyber capabilities transfer, we used the content normally visible to consumers—final responses, reasoning summaries, and tool interactions—as our baseline for distillation, and tested how much additional cyber capability transfers when the student has access to the teacher’s exact reasoning traces.

We started each training run from the same pretrained student model. We created a supervised fine-tuning dataset consisting primarily of trajectories from Astra-level teacher models working on coding and defensive cybersecurity tasks. Each trajectory includes all of the steps a model takes as it works through a task, including any tool interactions and its final response. We evaluated each student after fine-tuning and again after a lightweight round of reinforcement learning in cybersecurity and coding environments.

After supervised fine-tuning, the student trained on exact reasoning traces generally outperformed the student trained on reasoning summaries. After reinforcement learning, the exact-trace student still scored higher at the largest inference budget tested on both benchmarks shown, while the summary-trained student scored higher at lower budgets.1.

Our cyber distillation results suggest that protecting reasoning traces can limit cyber capability transfer, even when the underlying task is one allowed under our usage policies. Across many such interactions, exact reasoning traces can teach a student skills that generalize beyond the tasks the teacher originally performed. We will continue studying how much additional capability transfers across different student models and distillation training recipes.

According to recent reports, we defend against adversarial distillation at two complementary levels of our safeguard stack. At the request level, model behavior, classifier checks, and API controls limit reasoning trace extraction. At the campaign level, we look for patterns in request-level and account-level signals that can reveal coordinated extraction attempts. In turn, attacks uncovered in investigations become examples for training and testing our safeguards.

Our defenses against adversarial distillation combine safeguards for individual requests with campaign detection and enforcement. Findings from investigations and automated red-teaming help strengthen those safeguards.

Adversarial training teaches models to recognize reasoning extraction attempts and refuse to disclose protected reasoning, while preserving responses to legitimate requests for explanations and assistance. Adversarial training examples come from successful attacks identified through internal automated red-teaming, investigations, and responsible disclosures of potential security weaknesses from outside researchers or industry partners.

We use input classifiers to detect attempts to extract protected reasoning, and output classifiers to detect leaks of protected reasoning in assistant messages and tool-call arguments. These safeguards apply to both streaming and non-streaming responses.

In a recent development, tool-call coverage is crucial because a model can expose protected reasoning in a tool’s arguments without including it in its final answer. Output classifiers can block suspected leaks before that content reaches the caller.

API-level protections restrict how protected reasoning can be reused across interactions and models. Our September disclosure described attacks that moved encrypted reasoning from one conversation into another and asked the model to reveal the reasoning in user-readable form. We strengthened protections across user, workspace, organization, and model-family boundaries, including closing a pathway that could expose another user’s encrypted reasoning.

With GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol, we tie a model’s protected reasoning to the conversation history that produced it. As newly introduced messages are added, the model can build on its earlier reasoning. If an earlier message is rewritten, our API drops the reasoning that followed it⁠(opens in a new window). We also prevent older model families with weaker safeguards from reading GPT‑6.2 Astra and Sol’s protected reasoning.

When our systems detect unauthorized adversarial distillation campaigns, which often include coordinated attempts to extract our models’ reasoning, we investigate the accounts responsible. When we identify violations, we enforce against the network of accounts, consistent with our policies and terms of service. Through investigations of each campaign, we generate insights that allow us to upgrade our defenses in order to better detect similar activity. We also share indicators of compromise with other model providers so they can investigate related abuse on their own services.

Industry observers note that this work extends beyond our own platform. Our consistent-standards policy establishes shared standards for safeguards and coordinated enforcement across providers offering our models. We work closely with partners where appropriate to uphold these standards and strengthen protections across deployments.

Sharing relevant findings across industry and government where appropriate can help disrupt campaigns and enable model developers and providers to better identify and defend against attempts to distill frontier models.

To measure how well our request-level safeguards work together, we test whether attackers can still extract protected reasoning in a setup that closely mirrors production deployments of our models and safeguards. In static evaluations, we replay a fixed set of previously successful attacks to see which still expose protected reasoning. In adaptive evaluations, automated AI red-teamers adjust their approach based on how the system responds, which can uncover weaknesses the static tests miss.

In a recent development, we also vary what testers can see. Black-box testing gives them the same view an external user would have, while white-box testing gives them additional information about the system to help them develop stronger attacks. In our adaptive black-box evaluation, we tested whether attackers could recover protected reasoning the model had generated while answering an earlier request or the current one. On GPT‑6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards, the average attack success rate was below 1% for each attack type. Both rates were substantially lower than on GPT‑6 Astra with its original safeguards. We’re now applying selected safeguard improvements to GPT‑6 Astra as well.

GPT‑6 Astra defender with original safeguards.

GPT‑6.2 Astra defender with updated safeguards.

Extracting protected reasoning from an earlier request.

Extracting protected reasoning from the current request.

In a recent development, attack success rate (ASR) in adaptive black-box red-teaming against GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Astra, aggregated across six attacker models. Lower ASR is better.

In a recent development, we have seen multiple unauthorized adversarial distillation campaigns on our platform this year, and shared initial findings in our September report. Our weekly enforcement actions against these campaigns have ranged in scale from thousands to tens of thousands of accounts, with the rate increasing significantly this past summer.

In order to measure the effectiveness of our efforts, we also track the prevalence of distillation abuse, as well as the time between detection and enforcement. Our objective is to constrain the volume and value of the data distillers are able to obtain, to increase the cost of distillation campaigns, and to shorten the time needed to respond to upcoming attacks. We continue to improve these defenses through adversarial testing and investigations.

Adversarial distillation also poses a national security risk. A foreign actor that reproduces advanced capabilities from a U.S. model can deploy them without the protections its developer put in place. In February, we briefed⁠(opens in a new window) Congress on activity indicating that DeepSeek was attempting to distill U.S. frontier models. In September, we reported disrupting a campaign to extract our models’ protected reasoning and attributed a core part of that activity to individuals associated with Moonshot AI, the developer of Kimi. We plan to share more soon about recent campaigns we’ve disrupted.

We support legislation that would give the U.S. government more tools to identify and sanction foreign actors that illicitly extract capabilities from American AI models. We’ve also told Congress we support the Chip Security Act, the AI OVERWATCH Act, and the MATCH Act. Stronger export controls can limit adversaries’ access to the hardware needed to train frontier models. Distillation defenses make it harder to acquire some of the same capabilities from models already trained. Both efforts help maintain a U.S. lead in frontier AI, giving developers more room to slow a release when they need time to test safeguards.

It has been revealed that supporting the safe proliferation of frontier capabilities is an important goal of our anti-distillation work. Our experience so far suggests several useful steps that other model developers and platforms can take:.

Industry observers note that protect private reasoning across the full interaction. Check assistant messages and tool-call arguments for leaks, and restrict how encrypted reasoning can be reused across conversations and models.

According to recent reports, keep successful extraction attack logs found through red-teaming, production monitoring, or responsible disclosure as regression tests. Where appropriate, and consistent with applicable privacy policies, use those examples to improve model training and classifiers. When evaluating updated defenses, replay the original attacks and test whether an adaptive red-teamer can still find a way through those defenses.

Combine request-level mitigations with campaign-level investigation and enforcement.

Coordinate safeguard requirements and enforcement with deployment partners, and share expertise with other AI model developers, to ensure a high floor of distillation safeguards across the industry.

We have previously also shared findings through the Frontier Model Forum⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) and appropriate government information-sharing channels to help other developers strengthen their defenses while keeping the details attackers could exploit private. We’ll continue working with researchers, developers, and partners to share what we learn about emerging attacks and effective defenses.

As we make frontier AI broadly available, our defenses against adversarial distillation aim to reduce the risk that its capabilities are reproduced without adequate safeguards, supporting our mission to ensure that artificial general intelligence is deployed safely and benefits all of humanity.

According to recent reports, related work from Anthropic⁠(opens in a fresh window) reported a similar advantage when training on full reasoning transcripts rather than summaries on SWE-bench Verified, a software engineering benchmark. Our result indicates this advantage extends to frontier cybersecurity.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, Amazon CloudWatch reveals support for your own application telemetry in the CloudWatch Observability EKS add-on. The CloudWatch agent you already run now accepts metrics, traces, and logs from your applications, so you don't deploy and operate a separate collector to get them into CloudWatch.

Applications instrumented with an OpenTelemetry SDK send to an OTLP endpoint that the agent serves on every node, on by default. Metrics arrive as CloudWatch metrics you query with PromQL, traces go to AWS X-Ray and Transaction Search, and logs go to CloudWatch Logs.

For Prometheus metrics, the agent scrapes the targets described by standard ServiceMonitor and PodMonitor objects, with no Prometheus operator to run and no change to your scrape configuration. Each team defines its own targets alongside its application rather than in one central add-on configuration. Label selectors let you choose which monitors CloudWatch scrapes.

Both sources carry the same Kubernetes, host, cloud, and service attributes the add-on applies to the pod they came from, so you can join application telemetry to your cluster metrics.

In a recent development, custom telemetry is available in version 8.0.0 and later of the EKS add-on and Helm chart, in all AWS Regions where CloudWatch supports OpenTelemetry metrics. Telemetry is charged at the Amazon EKS OpenTelemetry ingestion rate of $0.08 per GB. For details, see Amazon CloudWatch insights pricing.

To get started, see Custom telemetry in the Amazon CloudWatch User Guide.

However, optimizing the harness of a memory system remains largely manual, and unrestricted editing alone does not ensure structural improvements. In this paper, we introduce HoMe, an evaluation-driven framework that iteratively evaluates candidate harnesses and derives each new candidate from any previously evaluated harness by editing any part of it. HoMe combines session-level memory versioning with execution traces to identify shared failure mechanisms across cases and localize them to the responsible sessions and harness components. It encourages early structural exploration through candidate gating and reduces evaluation cost through smoke tests, adaptive sampling, and the reuse of constructed memory. We validate HoMe with the open-source memory system ReMe on two large-scale long-horizon memory benchmarks, LongMemEval-S and BEAM. With six formal candidate evaluations per benchmark, after a full initial evaluation, HoMe discovers harnesses that improve end-task performance over the originally strong harness while consuming far fewer query-time tokens. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Holo4 is our new series of agentic models. It comes in two sizes: 27B dense and 35B-A3B Mixture of Experts. Both are available on the H Models API. We are also releasing an updated version of Holotron 3: Holotron4 Nano.

Holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs. It scores well on academic benchmarks, but we built it for real business workflows. It was trained through supervised and reinforcement learning on a large set of environments and tasks, including those generated by our Agentic Task Factory.

Sources indicate that holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools. It uses whichever fits the task. Most agentic models are trained for one interface only: GUI-focused models are blind without a screen, while models that prefer tool calling are stuck in front of an application that has no API. Real work is not siloed that way, and a single business task can require combining these different approaches.

Holo4 runs on desktops, on the web, on Android, in a code sandbox and against business APIs. It is the same model in each case and it is called the same way. You do not need to select a different model for each platform.

According to recent reports, holo4 models improve significantly over their Qwen base. Holo4 trails only the strongest closed models on long workflows: on OSWorld 2.0, Holo4 27B scores 61.7% against 81.8% for Opus 5.5, and Holo4 35B-A3B reaches 30.9%. However, it does so with orders of magnitude fewer parameters and at a much lower cost. We open-source every trajectory behind our scores on public benchmarks: replay each step at trajectories.hcompany.ai or download them from Hugging Face.

On the hardest academic benchmarks for desktop control (OSWorld 2.0) and API use (AutomationBench), Holo4 competes with frontier models at a much lower cost per task.

Our internal set of agentic pipelines builds interactive environments and verifiable tasks from documentation alone, such as screenshots of real websites or open-source software. So far it has produced about 10,000 tasks across web apps, MCP servers and desktop environments, including hybrid environments that expose the same state through a GUI and MCP.

Alongside training, we rebuilt our harness, the loop that executes the model's actions and manages its context over hundreds of steps, using feedback from agentic performance on OSWorld 2.0. Agents tagged why each task failed and engineers reviewed their fixes. The largest changes were giving the agent a reliable memory that can keep track of hundreds of steps, and a shell on the desktop machine itself.

Industry observers note that our post-training stack is designed to adapt to newly introduced foundation models and produce agents that generalize across interfaces and environments. As a member of the NVIDIA Nemotron Coalition, we applied our latest stack to the Nemotron 3 Nano Omni model as a follow-up to Holotron 3.

The same recipe turns Nemotron 3 Nano Omni into Holotron4 Nano, a generalist agentic model that significantly improves over the base model on GUI workflows and in environments exposing MCP, APIs or coding sandboxes.

Gains are absolute percentage-point improvements over Nemotron 3 Nano Omni.

These gains show that our recipe transfers well and can turn a generalist model into an agentic expert. Nothing in it is size-specific.

We show that for core structured editing regimes, an LLM optimizer is unnecessary, and introduce Forward Weight-Space Programming (FWSP): a deterministic pipeline combining probing, localization, stratified operators (O1-O4), automatic blind routing (83.3% vs. 33.3% for a 27B LLM with the same tool library), and paired verification with zero additional per-token computation. For reasoning LLMs, we propose Protected FisherGate, a closed-form covariance-whitened readout edit orthogonal to normal-reasoning states: on DeepSeek-R1-0528-8B, a single frozen math-calibrated patch achieves 84.2% HumanEval pass@1 (1K budget; 75.4 +/- 9.4% across 3/5 Stage-4-passing subsets), beating 512-token-reserved budget forcing by +14.6 pp (-23.4% tokens) while transferring across HF-to-vLLM backends on full GSM8K and MATH-500. Across five modalities and thirteen models (50K to 27B dense and FP8 MoE), we further prove and verify two operator boundaries, subspace entanglement and frozen representation span, where FWSP-localized LoRA bridges forward-only and gradient adaptation.

In a recent development, today, AWS announces the preview of Data Hub in AWS Billing and Cost Management, a managed data layer that enables AWS FinOps Agent to query cost and usage data with SQL. In preview, Data Hub is available to AWS FinOps Agent, so the agent can identify the individual resources behind a cost change, break down spend by team or cost allocation tag, and show how a resource's cost and usage change hour by hour. With AWS FinOps Agent and Data Hub, customers get these answers without setting up a data export or building and maintaining a cost data pipeline.

Data Hub provides 13 months of hourly, resource-level cost and usage data in the published CUR 2.0 schema, including resource identifiers and cost allocation tags. AWS provisions the data, refreshes data daily, and maintains the schema as new services, commitments, and charge types are added. When set up from the management account, Data Hub covers cost and usage data across the accounts in your organization.

Recent findings suggest that data Hub (preview) is available in the US East (N. Virginia) Region and covers cost and usage data across regions. There is no charge for Data Hub during preview.

In a recent development, to learn more about Data Hub, see the AWS Billing and Cost Management User Guide and the launch blog. You can get started from the Data Hub page in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console or from the AWS FinOps Agent console.
