Industry News: MPS in PyTorch 2.15

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1364 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that if you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15!
  • A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face.
  • If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that if you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and new Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.

Recent findings suggest that you'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:.

In a recent development, FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

You can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:.

In a recent development, every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each upcoming token goes through the model as a single row, so the big matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

According to recent reports, MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

According to recent reports, in 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The newly introduced Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:.

The decoding kernel shows up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:.

Working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:.

Recent findings suggest that small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

It has been revealed that audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them new paths through Metal:.

Recent findings suggest that token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:.

It has been revealed that one of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:.

According to recent reports, you can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:.

Several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

Work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

Sources indicate that once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:.

Scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

Industry observers note that the move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

Bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

PyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

A massive thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (301 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.33946v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: Automated decision systems, from learned policies to model-based optimizers, often minimize costs such as energy or resource use while meeting a service requirement, for example the quality of service (QoS) specified in a service level agreement (SLA), a comfort band, or a safety margin. The requirement can be scalarized with the costs into a single objective, with a fixed or an adaptively tuned (Lagrangian) weight, or it can be imposed as a constraint. We study this choice in the Smart Buildings Challenge, in which a single policy controls the heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) of previously unseen buildings and is evaluated by a weighted sum of comfort, energy cost and carbon emissions. With all other components fixed, we compare the two treatments in model-based optimization, represented by model predictive control (MPC) with the requirement as a hard or a soft (l1-penalized) constraint, and in learned policies, represented by proximal policy optimization (PPO) with a fixed or a Lagrangian penalty in the reward or a projection layer on the action. In MPC, the soft constraint reproduces the hard one once its weight exceeds the requirement's shadow price, which the challenge's comfort weight exceeds approximately fourfold; below this weight, comfort is sacrificed, and under a metric that values comfort below its shadow price the soft constraint outperforms the hard one by up to 28%. A weight tuned on the training buildings is 3.9% worse than the hard constraint on 48 unseen buildings, because the shadow price varies across buildings. In PPO, the projected policy satisfies the requirement from the outset and leads early in training; with longer training, the Lagrangian policy overtakes it while the projected policy deteriorates, and the fixed penalty does not learn to satisfy the requirement.

What Does Skill Lift Actually Measure? A Source-Code-Level Audit and Noise-Aware Reanalysis of SkillsBench

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (278 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.33943v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: Agent skills are directories of instructions, reference materials, and scripts loaded on demand by coding agents. According to SkillsBench, although human-curated skills can raise the passing rate by about 16.6 percentage points (pp) on average, they have actually reduced the results for some tasks. Later research has started to gate or eliminate skills according to the above per-task gains. We have audited the above benchmark at the source-code level and analysed 7,554 public trials to form 1,421 paired "(configuration, task) cells". Source-code audit identified two controlled-verified cases of grader dependence and one operational definition gap; the average lift on these three tasks was 74.6 pp, and the overall average lift for the full set was 18.7 pp. The audit also found that four tasks contained placeholder skill directories, and a certain execution harness additionally added 48 built-in skills in most runs. No task-level reduction achieved statistical significance in the pooled reanalysis with multiple-testing correction. As there were at most three runs per condition for each cell, the observed negative differences are very susceptible to run-sampling noise, and arithmetically, 58% of the cells could not have shown a decrease. Therefore, the raw numbers of negative cells cannot show that skills cause harm. A gating strategy based on the skill-free score seems to improve by 2-3 pp in the logs; however, even after shuffling condition labels to remove any skill effect, it still achieves an increase of 4-7 pp. On the held-out runs not used for fitting and decision-making, there was no statistically significant improvement. The audit ledger and analysis scripts have been published by us.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that AWS Network Firewall reveals the public preview of automated internet firewall (Preview), a newly introduced centralized control that allows you to configure Network Firewall, with native network address translation (NAT) capability, on the internet gateways of all the Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs) in your environment.
  • AWS Network Firewall is a stateful, managed, network firewall and intrusion detection and prevention service for your VPC.
  • Industry observers note that to help you get started swiftly, automated internet firewall comes with a default security policy, which uses Amazon managed rule groups including active threat defense that uses AWS unique threat intelligence to protect your workloads against evolving threats on the internet.

Sources indicate that AWS Network Firewall reveals the public preview of automated internet firewall (Preview), a newly introduced centralized control that allows you to configure Network Firewall, with native network address translation (NAT) capability, on the internet gateways of all the Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs) in your environment. Using automated internet firewall (Preview) mode, you can centrally define your Network Firewall security rules and enforce them on all inbound and outbound traffic across the internet gateways of your VPCs. You are not required to make routing or architectural changes to deploy automated internet firewall (Preview). You can deploy it across select VPCs or your entire account, organization or organization unit.

AWS Network Firewall is a stateful, managed, network firewall and intrusion detection and prevention service for your VPC. Customers use it to inspect their traffic and secure AWS resources. Prior to this launch, customers would configure AWS Network Firewalls inside their VPCs in the traffic path of all internet communication to achieve thorough security coverage against the threats on the internet. They deployed Network Firewall endpoints in dedicated subnets and made route updates for every subnet that needed internet access across all their VPCs. In addition, they monitored the environment to ensure that no new internet network paths bypassed these security controls. Automated internet firewall (Preview) makes this deployment and management simpler. You just define and maintain filtering rules, and AWS enforces it directly at the internet gateway of every VPC in scope, ensuring that all intended traffic entering or leaving your VPCs via the internet gateway is inspected. Automated Internet firewall comes with built-in NAT functionality for your egress-only internet connectivity needs. You can use it to filter traffic, perform NAT and log all internet activity across all internet gateways. You don't need to make architectural changes inside every VPC or monitor every internet network path. Automated Internet firewall (Preview) allows you the option to automatically extend your organization's security policy to all future VPCs and subnets at creation.

Industry observers note that to help you get started swiftly, automated internet firewall comes with a default security policy, which uses Amazon managed rule groups including active threat defense that uses AWS unique threat intelligence to protect your workloads against evolving threats on the internet. You can also create your own custom rule groups or use any of the managed rule groups from AWS Marketplace with automated internet firewall.

AWS Network Firewall operating in automated internet firewall mode (Preview) is available in preview in all AWS Regions except MXP, AWS GovCloud, and China. To learn more, visit the Network Firewall documentation and see the AWS Network Firewall pricing page. To get started, visit the Amazon VPC or Network Security Manager console.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

Here's what changed, and what's next:.

Sources indicate that the core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:.

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:.

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:.

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too major to run on the device with the same session code:.

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

Reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the latest provider can't replay them.

It has been revealed that API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

According to recent reports, while we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:.

The first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:.

And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

Language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.33909v1 Announce Type: fresh Abstract: Medical reasoning agents combine foundation models with specialized tools to interpret medical images, yet reusing their historical experience remains challenging. A correct final answer can conceal flawed reasoning or tool use, synthesized advice may lack source support, and superficially similar cases may require different diagnostic procedures. In this paper, we propose EGSE, an evidence-grounded skill evolution framework that distills historical dialogues from similar cases into reusable conditional workflows and progressively refines a multi-faceted skill library through supported and validated updates to improve medical agents. EGSE evaluates intermediate reasoning and tool use and contrasts repeated successful and failed rollouts to extract useful practices and evidence-supported avoidance guidance. These experiences are synthesized into workflows with applicability conditions and checks traceable to source dialogues. Library additions and merges require source-grounded review and execution validation. At inference time, EGSE routes queries to skill nodes organized by imaging modality, question task type, and disease category, then retrieves and selects applicable workflows based on their conditions, the current images, and the question to guide evidence acquisition and interpretation. Experiments across four chest X-ray benchmarks show that EGSE outperforms representative medical agents and skill evolution methods in reasoning accuracy while reducing tool calls. It also delivers consistent accuracy gains across seven foundation models and supports skill transfer across datasets.

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.33897v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Medical reasoning agents combine large language model (LLM) reasoning with clinical workflows and specialized neural tools. However, general-purpose LLMs receive limited training exposure to domain-specific medical tools, and the uncertainty and distributional shifts of neural tool outputs make selecting tools from simple descriptions significantly more challenging than in deterministic settings such as calculators or dictionary lookups. In this paper, we propose EATS, an experience-augmented tool selection strategy that leverages accumulated tool-use trajectories to improve tool selection in medical reasoning agents. EATS constructs a memory of past interactions, including queries, tool choices, arguments, and self-evaluated feedback, and retrieves relevant experiences to guide tool selection for new queries. As memory construction does not require ground-truth supervision, EATS scales naturally with test-time experience. We evaluate EATS on tool-augmented medical reasoning tasks, including closed-ended visual question answering and free-form report generation. Experiments on four public datasets, ChestAgentBench, CheXbench, MIMIC-CXR, and SLAKE-VQA, across three multimodal LLMs, Qwen3-VL 2B, Qwen3-VL 32B, and GPT-5.5, show consistent gains in tool selection behavior and downstream medical reasoning performance. Code is available at https://github.com/Limingyuan001/EATS.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that AWS Lambda now publishes Event Function state change events to Amazon EventBridge.
  • In a recent development, customers use Lambda Event Functions to build APIs, event processing workloads, multi-step workflows, and data pipelines.
  • This feature is available in all commercial AWS Regions.

Recent findings suggest that AWS Lambda now publishes Event Function state change events to Amazon EventBridge. Lambda emits an event each time an Event Function version changes state because of a customer action, such as creating, updating, publishing, or deleting a function. These events help platform and DevOps teams to trigger automation as soon as a function becomes ready to invoke, an enhancement finishes, or an operation fails, without polling the GetFunction API.

In a recent development, customers use Lambda Event Functions to build APIs, event processing workloads, multi-step workflows, and data pipelines. As organizations grow to thousands of functions, platform teams need to know when a function changes state so they can take the next step. For example, a deployment pipeline can run integration tests and then shift alias traffic once a upcoming version becomes active. Until now, these tools had to poll the GetFunction API to track state changes. Polling consumed API quota, slowed down pipelines, and required custom retry logic, which added operational overhead. With this launch, you can create EventBridge rules that match on fields such as the function ARN, detail type, or state, and route matched events to targets such as AWS Step Functions, AWS Lambda, Amazon SNS, or Amazon SQS. This helps you build reliable, event-driven deployment pipelines across all of your functions, without writing or maintaining custom polling logic.

This feature is available in all commercial AWS Regions. You can create rules by using the EventBridge console, AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), AWS SDKs, AWS CloudFormation, AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK), or AWS Serverless Application Model (AWS SAM). Lambda publishes these events automatically at no additional cost. Standard pricing applies to the targets that your EventBridge rules invoke. To learn more, see the AWS Lambda Developer Guide and the Amazon EventBridge User Guide.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

Industry observers note that TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

Sources indicate that TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

The catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch people had to work harder to get in.

Industry observers note that until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

In a recent development, to make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

TorchTPU adds TPU as a latest backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:.

According to recent reports, the extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

Industry observers note that transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

The model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

It has been revealed that TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

Models too massive for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:.

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1.

According to recent reports, the Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:.

According to recent reports, the bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

It has been revealed that decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

We're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

In a recent development, the Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

It's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an concern on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 issues, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel intends. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch users. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

It has been revealed that we can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an issue and tell us about it.

FORK: Co-Evolving Safe Disclosure and Decision Skills Against Attackers Who Read Every Refusal

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (199 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.33879v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: When a guardrail rejects an LLM agent's action, its message reaches any attacker observing the trajectory: a fixed refusal leaves benign users unable to recover, whereas an explanation can tell the attacker what to try next. We study this as safe disclosure: explaining rejections so that authorized tasks recover without increasing adaptive attack success. Safe disclosure depends on both the decision and the message: what the guardrail blocks and what it reveals to the agent and the attacker. Because hand-written rules alone cannot anticipate how adaptive attackers probe decisions or use messages, we introduce FORK, which co-evolves a guardrail's natural-language decision and disclosure skills with an attacker that reads every public message. Each exploited message and permissive decision gives FORK evidence for a gradient-free revision of its natural-language skill library. We evaluate FORK on four benchmarks. Averaged over three agents on FORK-World, FORK cuts attack success rate (ASR) under adaptive attack from 78.4% to 14.1% and keeps utility above 85%, outperforming baselines on both ASR and utility. Notably, on MT-AgentRisk, whose environments and tasks are unseen in training, FORK lowers ASR from 70.6% to 9.1% with 93.1% benign utility.

Can Its Own Misses Teach an MLLM to Find Small Brain Metastases?

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (253 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.33836v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are becoming general readers of medical images, yet they remain weak at locating small abnormalities. Brain metastases expose this gap: at 384 px a 0.1 mL lesion covers less than a quarter of one visual token, and at one false positive per scan frontier MLLMs find fewer than 30% of lesions of 0.1-1 mL. Fine-tuning on one dataset helps but transfers poorly, and improving it further is slow trial and error steered by a single score. We introduce LANTERN (Lesion-finding AgeNt Through Error-driven Recursive learNing), a framework in which an MLLM improves recursively from its own misses. LANTERN recasts model development as an error-driven loop: a failure census attributes every missed lesion to one of four causes, an LLM mentor revises one of four levels (evidence acquisition, visual representation, learning policy, decision aggregation) per round, and a rule frozen before the first round decides what is kept, without test data and with every tool call audited. Over 15 unattended rounds, LANTERN raises a fine-tuned 4B MLLM from finding 75% to 94% of lesions at one false positive per scan on BraTS-MET, and 91% of those of 0.1-1 mL, compared with at most 51% and 29% for five frontier MLLMs read under the starting protocol; the gains hold on an external cohort (89%) and on unseen meningiomas (77%). These results show that an MLLM's own misses, attributed to their causes, can drive its reliable recursive self-improvement.

According to recent reports, amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) for Oracle now provides a Primary Endpoint, a DNS name that always resolves to the current primary DB instance in a replica configuration. When you switch over to an Oracle replica, Amazon RDS points the Primary Endpoint to the new primary DB instance, so you don't need to change your application connection strings. Previously, after each switchover, you had to update connection strings or DNS records to point to the new primary DB instance, which often required change approvals and coordination across teams.

According to recent reports, with Primary Endpoint, you can run planned switchovers, such as disaster recovery drills, to replicas in the same AWS Region or to cross-Region replicas without changing your application configuration. If your applications connect through the Primary Endpoint, you don't need to update their connection strings after the switchover.

Industry observers note that every RDS for Oracle Enterprise Edition DB instance has a Primary Endpoint at no additional charge, and you don't have to create it. The Primary Endpoint is provided in addition to the instance endpoint, so your existing applications aren't affected.

Industry observers note that primary Endpoint is available in all commercial AWS Regions where Amazon RDS for Oracle is available. To learn more, see Using the Primary Endpoint for Amazon RDS for Oracle in the Amazon RDS User Guide.

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1295 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow.
  • Sources indicate that this post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience.
  • Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.

Sources indicate that this post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:.

Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.

The Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda. The torch_neuronx package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating New Backend Integration by PrivateUse1.

You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:.

According to recent reports, the modes parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The capture_enabled_for_nc parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting correlate_device_time=True propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages() table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available ProfileMode values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation.

Neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what key_averages() reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.

Industry observers note that after profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched .neff and .ntff files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching .neff and .ntff files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions.

For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.

You profile three implementations of the same operation:.

The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.

All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the torch-neuronx examples directory.

Start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.

Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:.

The schedule uses wait=2, warmup=1, and active=1 across four prof.step() calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.

According to recent reports, call torch.neuron.synchronize() inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.

After profiling finishes, inspect the key_averages() table. Sort by self_privateuse1_time_total to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full key_averages() output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.

The key averages table reveals that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.

Sources indicate that the table highlights which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. aten::mul has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.

Each row maps directly to the function. aten::mul runs for x * x, x * rms, and the final multiplication by weight. aten::mean reduces the last dimension. aten::add adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. aten::rsqrt computes the reciprocal square root.

Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.

Recent findings suggest that in Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule, and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running.

Industry observers note that the system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:.

In eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow aten::mul.Tensor from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.

The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.

It has been revealed that replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in rms_norm function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:.

The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.

The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.

Sources indicate that in the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.

For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with torch.compile.

In a recent development, with @torch.compile(backend="neuron"), TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.

The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table.

The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution.

Recent findings suggest that the table demonstrates one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to torch.rms_norm, at 375 μs compared with 403 μs.

Industry observers note that both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as x_sq and mean_sq between separately dispatched operations.

In a recent development, key_averages() shows which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes.

You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost.

Sources indicate that in Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound.

The front door to AI in the workplace.

In a recent development, open models like Gemma 4 from Google DeepMind are a great option to keep your data local. But how can a local AI model integrate with on-premises data?

Sources indicate that alloyDB Omni, Google’s 100% PostgreSQL-compatible database that runs anywhere, now integrates with locally hosted large language models (LLMs). With AlloyDB Omni, you can build agentic experiences on your own infrastructure and on your own terms. Whether it’s in the cloud, in your datacenter, or even on your laptop, you can have data plus AI anywhere.

AlloyDB Omni is a downloadable, run-anywhere edition of AlloyDB that easily deploys to your own infrastructure, including on-premises. AlloyDB Omni packs powerful, built-in AI, including the same ScaNN indexing technology powering Google Search. When you pair AlloyDB Omni with a model, you can store vector embeddings at scale; search them semantically; and even query the database using natural language. You can use virtually any model you like, whether that’s a frontier Cloud-hosted model like Gemini or a local model. And with locally hosted models you maintain complete control over your data environment.

You can now connect AlloyDB Omni to local models like Gemma 4 and Qwen3.8. No matter which model you choose, the architecture remains the same.

AlloyDB Omni calls a local model server directly from SQL — keeping prompts, data, and responses inside your environment.

In a recent development, this setup enables entirely fresh use cases for environments that were previously blocked from adopting agentic capabilities. If you operate an air-gapped network or have data locality requirements, you can still build intelligent applications. You can analyze local logs, generate summaries of proprietary internal documents, and power localized chatbots—all while maintaining strict data governance.

Keep data on-premises: Because the database and the model sit in the same local environment, your data never crosses the public internet.

Reduce latency: Processing inference requests locally minimizes network transit time.

It has been revealed that query directly via SQL: Your standard database queries can invoke machine learning functions that process data locally. Like this:.

Next, you’ll see how to run queries like this yourself, step by step.

You can test this integration on your own machines today. Using a Kubernetes environment we will show you how to deploy and integrate AlloyDB Omni and a local open model.

It has been revealed that in this example, we will use Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) to host the AlloyDB Omni database and local model. GKE gives us a standardized, reproducible environment but you can use the same setup on-prem or almost anywhere.

We will assume you have already setup:.

Kubernetes tools kubectl and Helm.

We will use the AlloyDB Omni Kubernetes operator to set up our AlloyDB Omni database. The Operator makes deploying and maintaining AlloyDB Omni a breeze.

Don’t forget to enable the googleMLExtension.

#42989. A global week for FinTech with 15 deals across 12 markets

A global week for FinTech with 15 deals across 12 markets

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4380 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fintech

⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It was a diverse week for FinTech deals this week, with 12 different countries home to at least one deal.
  • Sources indicate that there were a total of 15 FinTech deals this week, with a combined capital pool of $614m.
  • One of the most notable aspects of this week’s deals is the global reach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was a diverse week for FinTech deals this week, with 12 different countries home to at least one deal.

Sources indicate that there were a total of 15 FinTech deals this week, with a combined capital pool of $614m. This represented a slight downturn on the previous week, which saw $991m raised across 17 deals.

One of the most notable aspects of this week’s deals is the global reach. Typically, the US dominates the space and often accounts for more than half of deals. While the US still took the top spot for deals, there were just three. The only other place to record multiple deals was the UK, with two.

Sources indicate that the lion share of funding this week was attributed to just two deals, both of which secured over $200m. US-based Sanctuary Wealth’s $250m growth capital round was the biggest deal of the week. It plans to use the capital to expand its specialist expertise, win newly introduced business and complete acquisitions. Germany-based Pliant was a close second, securing €200m ($218.7m).

According to recent reports, sweden-based Trustly, which offers account-to-account payments built on Open Banking infrastructure, was the third biggest deal of the week, closing on $60m. The remaining FinTech deals this week were all $20m and under.

In terms of location, the other two US companies were Supertake and Metano, while the UK-based FinTechs were Acorda and Napo.

Europe had a strong week for deals. In addition to the UK, Germany and Sweden, there were also deals in Norway (Audun) and Spain (Reversa).

There were two deals in the middle east, with the UAE’s Sooner and Jordan’s invoiceQ. South America also had two FinTech deals, with Brazil’s IKKB and Argentina’s Lemon both closing deals. Finishing off the deals of the week were two deals in south Asia with India-based Ionic Wealth and Pakistan-based Neem.

Recent findings suggest that with the US’ weekly dominance in deal activity it is easy to assume it would also dominate in deal size. However, research from FinTech Global this week found that seven different countries were represented among the top 10 FinTech deals in Q1 – Q3 2026.

As for subsectors, WealthTech reigned supreme with four deals in total. The WealthTech companies were Sanctuary Wealth, Supertake, Ionic Wealth and Lemon. It was followed close behind by the infrastructure and enterprise software space, which recorded three deals. These were invoiceQ, IKKBand Neem.

In a recent development, as for the other subsectors, there were two deals apiece in PayTech (Pliant and Trustly), RegTech (Acorda and Reversa) and marketplace lending (Sooner and Audun). Finishing off, there was one deal each in CyberTech (Metano) and InsurTech (Napo).

Here are the 15 FinTech deals covered on FinTech Global this week:.

Sanctuary Wealth has received a $250m growth capital commitment from its existing backer Kennedy Lewis Investment Management.

The deal hands Sanctuary a larger pool of money to finance the ambitions, equity sales and succession prepares of the firms on its platform.

The fresh funding will be used to widen the specialist expertise available to Sanctuary’s Partner Firms, helping them serve clients across a broader range of needs, win newly introduced business and complete acquisitions.

Sanctuary will also gain more room to supply capital directly to Partner Firm owners, whether they want to fund expansion, cash out part of their stake or get ready for a leadership handover.

Kennedy Lewis, a multi-strategy private credit manager overseeing roughly $40bn in assets, has structured its commitment as $50m in mandatory convertible debt alongside a $200m delayed-draw term loan.

In addition, the investor has chosen to turn its current outstanding convertible debt holding in Sanctuary into equity. The relationship between the two firms dates back to 2022, and since that first investment Sanctuary has doubled its count of Partner Firms and nearly tripled the assets on its platform.

According to recent reports, over eight years, Sanctuary has built a platform designed to help advisors leaving wirehouses establish their own independent businesses. Its scale and depth have drawn growing attention from advisors and independent wealth managers, prompting the company to introduce additional affiliation models that give sophisticated advisors greater choice in how they pursue their goals.

Pliant, the Berlin-based B2B payments FinTech, has lined up more than €200m in fresh debt financing capacity across three separate deals with Ascory Bank AG and Viola Credit.

The new capacity is aimed at backing rising credit card transaction volumes and the credit lines Pliant extends to customers throughout Europe.

Commercial card issuing has particular liquidity demands, chiefly the need to fund customer credit balances and to post collateral for card scheme settlement. The new structures provide secured financing against both of these needs, allowing Pliant to handle larger volumes of transactions without compromising the efficiency of its funding model.

Two of the three deals come from Ascory Bank, which has partnered with Pliant for several years. One is a securitisation backed by receivables from Pliant’s European corporate credit card operations. The other covers the collateral needed for Visa’s settlement process, known as the Visa Prefunding Solution, giving Pliant the liquidity to keep pace with growing card activity.

According to recent reports, the third deal expands Pliant’s current growth debt facility with Viola Credit and includes an option to raise the amount available. Taken together, the agreements are expected to underpin Pliant’s planned European growth for a minimum of two years.

According to recent reports, the debt package comes shortly after Pliant revealed an $80m Series C round, which is earmarked for international expansion and further work on its AI-powered payment infrastructure. The new facilities sit alongside that equity investment, adding capacity specifically for the European commercial card business.

Founded in 2020, Pliant runs a modular B2B payments platform that brings together commercial card issuing, payment accounts, FX and spend management for both businesses and AI agents. Its customers span travel, e-commerce, insurance and AI-native technology, while FinTechs, software platforms and banks build their own commercial payment products on its infrastructure. Through its API-first platform, AI agents and applications can tap into regulated payment rails with permissions, controls and auditability included.

Trustly, the Stockholm-headquartered Pay by Bank specialist, has secured $60m in fresh capital as it moves to reposition payment data as a source of commercial intelligence for the merchants it serves.

According to FinSMEs, Nordic Capital, Alfvén & Didrikson and BlackRock all participated in the round. The Swedish firm prepares to channel the money into building new AI-powered products designed to extract insight from transaction flows.

Its stated aim is to give businesses sharper tools for attracting customers, keeping them engaged over a longer period and anticipating risk before it materialises.

It has been revealed that the raise marks a notable strategic direction for the firm. Rather than treating a payment as the end point of a transaction, Trustly intends to use the data generated at checkout as a lever for growth and protection, a shift that could change how merchants evaluate their payment providers.

Trustly offers account-to-account payments built on Open Banking infrastructure, allowing consumers to pay directly from their bank accounts with speed and security, in real time. Its network links more than 9,000 merchants with in excess of 650 million consumers, drawing on connections to 12,000 banks across upwards of 30 markets. Well-known names including PayPal, Virgin Media O2 and Booking.com count among its partners.

Supertake, a platform that uses AI agents to convert people’s market beliefs into stock portfolios, has secured $20m in seed funding to scale its business.

Venture firm Adjacent, through Nico Wittenborn, led the investment, with Coinbase Ventures and Union Square Ventures (USV) also taking part, according to a report from TechCrunch.

A number of angel investors joined the round, among them Nat Friedman, at the moment head of product at Meta Superintelligence Labs, Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch, product manager Nikita Bier, investor Scott Belsky and Nemil Dalal, a former Coinbase executive now serving as a visiting partner at Y Combinator.

The latest capital comes after a $2m pre-seed round.

Supertake intends to use the money to grow its headcount across functions such as engineering, design and growth marketing.

In a recent development, supertake’s stated mission is to make investing a meritocracy. Customers describe a conviction in everyday language, such as “Everyone will be on peptides”, and the platform builds an investment strategy around it, which is then run by frontier AI agents. Any user anywhere can follow and share these strategies, meaning ideas are judged on their performance rather than on whether their creator has time to monitor markets constantly.

Sooner, a UAE home-buying platform that funds half of a buyer’s down payment, has secured $20m in seed funding as it sets out to change how residents of the country purchase property.

The round drew backing from Nuwa Capital, Amwal Capital Partners, 500 Global, Annex Investments, Alserkal Group, Axeed LLC, Plus VC (+VC), 21 Ventures and Iliad Partners, along with a group of angel investors.

The startup is tackling a long-standing hurdle in the UAE property market, where purchasing a home has traditionally required buyers to find 20% of the price in cash upfront. Under Sooner’s model, buyers contribute 10% at the outset while the company covers the remaining half of the deposit using its own capital. That portion is then paid back in monthly instalments alongside the buyer’s mortgage over a term of between 12 and 60 months.

With the new capital in place, Sooner is aiming to facilitate more than AED 1bn worth of home purchases during 2027. The firm describes this target as an initial step towards helping a generation of tenants move into ownership.

In a recent development, sooner focuses on salaried buyers living in the UAE who want to purchase a ready-built property in Dubai. The process begins with a roughly two-minute check that highlights customers which homes fall within their budget, without affecting their credit score. The tech giant then arranges a first-time buyer mortgage pre-approval with a suitable bank, supported by a lowest mortgage rate guarantee, and approves the down payment support. Buyers can then book viewings through the platform and complete the purchase of their chosen property.

Ionic Wealth, a technology-driven wealth management platform owned by Angel One, has secured Rs177 crore ($19m) in a strategic funding round to power its next stage of expansion.

The round was backed by Angel One alongside a group of marquee families, and brings the total amount raised by the organization to around Rs466 crore ($50m).

It has been revealed that all investors from the earlier round returned for this one. The investor base includes prominent business families, Bollywood personalities, FinTech entrepreneurs, global CXOs, board advisors and media houses.

The investment follows a period of rapid growth. Within two years, Ionic Wealth has pushed its assets under management (AUM) beyond Rs16,000 crore. It now serves more than 2,900 high-net-worth and ultra-high-net-worth clients across over 12 cities, with a team of more than 100 private bankers.

Ionic Wealth plans to use the fresh capital to strengthen its portfolio-led proposition and global capabilities, bring AI into its WealthTech experience, grow its UHNI business and widen its presence both in India and overseas.

In a recent development, the tech giant described the funds as patient capital, which will let it build on its early bets. These include using technology to scale its HNI offering, advancing global investing through GIFT City, opening up fractional access through the Accredited Investor framework and SIFs, and creating a distinct UHNI offering for India’s leading families.

Sources indicate that operating under the Ionic Wealth brand, Angel One Wealth Limited is a wholly owned subsidiary of Angel One Limited, one of India’s major FinTech platforms with a user base of over 40 million. Ionic Wealth is an omnichannel WealthTech platform that aims to rethink wealth management for India’s emerging HNIs and UHNIs.

Recent findings suggest that it gives clients access to exclusive investment opportunities across asset classes, a round-the-clock digital experience through its app, and domain specialists who build strategic looks suited to each client’s wealth journey. The firm uses technology to generate sharper insights, boost team productivity and support scale.

Metano has come out of stealth with $12m in seed capital as enterprises struggle to keep autonomous software under control across their technology estates.

Sierra Ventures headed the round, which also drew backing from Correlation Ventures, High Alpha and 360 ONE.

The business is led by co-founders Neelima Rustagi, who serves as CEO, and Ratnesh Pandey, its CTO, with the leadership team bringing security backgrounds from ServiceNow, Zscaler, Palo Alto Networks, FireEye and Microsoft.

In a recent development, the launch lands at a moment when companies are rolling out AI agents on employee devices, in coding tools, across cloud systems and inside SaaS applications. Each new deployment widens a scattered attack surface.

Current security products tend to guard a single layer of infrastructure, leaving teams without the end-to-end view and behavioural insight required to protect agents that move between those layers on their own.

AI agents also differ from traditional software because they act and decide on the fly, frequently with valid credentials and sanctioned tools. Their conduct can shift depending on the prompts they receive, the outside material they consume and the conditions they run in, so dangers may stay hidden during early testing and only surface later.

Metano tackles this by merging three functions into a single control layer. First, it locates both sanctioned and shadow AI agents, along with MCP servers, skills and software packages, and maps the permissions and exposure attached to each.

Second, it interprets agent conduct through Hive, a live context graph that links tasks, identities, tools, data access and actions over the course of a session, allowing analysts to spot anomalies and judge whether an agent is acting in line with its purpose.

Third, it applies guardrails directly where agents run, including activity that never passes through conventional network gateways, so centrally set policies can halt harmful actions in the moment. The platform is designed to scale alongside a manufacturer’s maturity in deploying agents.

invoiceQ has secured $5m in a Series A round that surpassed its original fundraising goal, giving it fresh capital as governments across its markets push businesses towards mandatory digital invoicing.

Manara Ventures and Next Ventures co-led the investment. They were joined by Orange Ventures, the Innovative Startups and SMEs Fund (ISSF) and the Jordan Small and Medium Enterprises Fund (SME Fund Jo), with the latter now backing the tech giant for a second time.

The business already counts over 1,400 corporate customers and has built up a substantial set of regulatory credentials. It holds qualification from Saudi Arabia’s Zakat, Tax and Customs Authority (ZATCA) and meets the requirements of Jordan’s Income and Sales Tax Department (ISTD). The UAE Federal Tax Authority (FTA) and the Oman Tax Authority (OTA) have both recognised it as an Approved Service Provider (ASP), and it also operates as a certified Peppol Access Point (AP) and Service Metadata Publisher (SMP).

Recent findings suggest that mohannad Tobal, Mohammad Bassit, Fadi Al Jabali and Amer Ayyad established invoiceQ, which offers a cloud-based SaaS platform that allows companies to automatically generate, handle, send and store invoices that satisfy tax rules, all from a single system. Its technology connects with existing ERP, POS, accounting, e-commerce, banking and payment software, meaning clients can meet regulatory obligations without overhauling the tools they already rely on.

Audun, an AI-native debt collection start-up, has secured $3m in pre-seed funding as it sets out to overhaul one of the most manual corners of financial services.

The round drew support from Alliance VC, Y Combinator, Robinhood Ventures, Skyfall Ventures and FirstDegree, along with a group of angel investors.

Recent findings suggest that audun is taking a different route from most innovators in the space. For years, change in debt collection has largely meant building software and selling it to collection agencies. Rather than offering another product of that kind, Audun has set itself up as a licensed agency in its own right. It is already recovering money for clients using its own platform, which handles every stage of a case, from the opening reminder through to the final payment.

In a recent development, the company argues that technology is moving faster than ever, yet collection practices look much as they did two decades ago. In its view, every debtor is pushed through an identical routine, while case handlers are tied up with repetitive admin. Audun believes the distance between what technology makes possible and what the sector actually provides is now wider than at any point before.

Audun’s platform takes over the routine, administrative side of collection so that its staff can devote their attention to the conversations where human judgement matters most.

IKKB, a financial management platform for companies operating across borders, has closed a $3m seed round to secure regulatory licences and develop fresh products for its multi-currency business account.

According to recent reports, the investment was led by Canary. According to the announcement, the capital will help IKKB obtain the licences it needs to operate as a regulated institution in each of its markets. It will also fund further products built on top of the core account. The firm already has licensing applications under way in Brazil, the US and Canada.

Canary mentioned it first met co-founders Edward Konig and Rafael Katalan in August 2025 and tracked their progress for over a year before investing. The investor said the pair learned quickly, made difficult decisions with long-term goals in mind and achieved a great deal on limited funding. Canary believes a growing number of companies now operate internationally from launch, while the financial infrastructure supporting them remains slow, costly and fragmented.

According to recent reports, IKKB’s offering has grown considerably in a short time. Just over a year ago, its product had a single function, converting PIX payments into US dollars. It has since become a multi-currency account for businesses, holding balances in BRL, USD, EUR and MXN. The account connects to local payment rails in Brazil, the US, Europe and Mexico, and offers corporate cards in BRL and USD. The team developed the platform internally on modest capital and prioritised regulatory work from the outset.

The firm is focused on giving Latin American businesses a global account. Firms can manage international payments, foreign exchange and treasury from a single platform. The service operates on stablecoin rails and applies AI to provide additional services alongside the account. IKKB offers accounts, cards, currency exchange, payments and treasury management.

Acorda, a London-based anti-fraud startup set up by three former Monzo employees, has secured £1.8m in a pre-seed round as it builds a network that lets banks and payment providers pool scam intelligence.

Sources indicate that according to DealRoom, Eileen Burbidge has backed the round. The startup will put the capital towards bringing banks and payment firms onto its data-sharing network.

The platform gives financial institutions a secure way to exchange scam risk indicators linked to the person or business receiving a payment, in the moments before the funds leave the sender’s account.

In a recent development, with this information, the sending bank can judge how risky the recipient is before releasing the transfer. Acorda’s aim is to reduce the number of scams that succeed while also lowering the volume of legitimate payments wrongly flagged as fraudulent.

Acorda operates a fraud data-sharing network designed for banks and payment providers, focused on preventing scams at the point of payment rather than identifying losses once money has already moved.

Reversa, a Madrid-based RegTech firm developing artificial intelligence agents to handle regulatory tasks for businesses and public bodies, has secured €750,000 in fresh capital, which includes a pre-seed round headed by Itnig.

Itnig, the investment vehicle of the founders of Factorial, led the pre-seed portion of the raise. The Jobandtalent co-founders also joined, as did angel investors drawn from the legal and technology industries, among them executives at HappyRobot, Fuse Energy and several multinational banking and energy groups. Reversa also receives backing from Enisa and from the Neotec programme run by CDTI.

It has been revealed that the latest capital will help Reversa widen the international reach of its regulatory infrastructure and develop sector-focused products on top of it, targeting areas including financial services, energy and real estate. On the urban planning side, the firm is developing agents designed to streamline land-use permits, a recognised obstacle to building new homes. Hiring across engineering, product and sales is also planned.

Reversa’s platform features a regulatory radar, through which agents link directly to official sources, assess how each regulatory change affects a business and support the steps needed to put it into practice. The technology also tackles operational and commercial challenges, such as pinpointing which legal framework applies when a company enters a new market, or automating compliance checks on a new product.

Customers also use it for jurisdiction-specific legal research and for drafting and revising contracts and policies. For public affairs teams, the agents track legislative procedures in real time, helping organisations prepare for upcoming rule changes and engage with the lawmaking process.

In a recent development, great Lakes, which holds an A+ rating from AM Best, will provide the capacity, while ERGO Travel Insurance Services Ltd, part of Munich Re company ERGO Group, will oversee the arrangement as MGA under delegated authority from Great Lakes. All fresh business from 5 November 2026 falls under the partnership, and renewals will transfer from the same date.

The deal came after Great Lakes reviewed Napo’s underwriting proposition and business looks, and it gives the pet insurer long-term capacity supported by an A+ financial strength rating as it expands.

Recent findings suggest that alongside the capacity agreement, Napo has added newly introduced cover options underwritten by Great Lakes. Its lifetime range now includes 40 options, with yearly vet fee limits between £2,000 and £16,000, plus a choice of excess and co-pay.

Mercia Ventures, an existing backer, led the funding round. IW Capital and Advantage Insurance Organization Limited took part as fresh investors, and DN Capital and Companion Fund, the pet-care venture arm of Mars Petcare, made follow-on investments.

According to recent reports, the manufacturer did not disclose the size of the round. Napo looks to direct the capital towards further automation in pricing and claims and towards expanding its direct distribution.

Jean-Philippe Doumeng co-founded Napo in 2021 and named the company after his dachshund, Napoleon. He set it up because many pet owners do not realise how fast veterinary costs rise until their animal is sick or hurt, and by then it can be too late to buy a policy.

According to recent reports, napo handles pricing, claims and customer service in-house and applies AI where it makes cover fairer. Its machine-learning pricing models draw on the manufacturer’s own policy and claims data, local vet costs and an AI-generated health profile covering more than 500 breeds. This approach lets Napo price rarer breeds on their individual traits instead of automatically classing them as high risk, and it can detect patterns such as how a dachshund’s risk shifts as it ages.

Tether, the largest company in the digital asset sector, has made an investment in Lemon, an Argentine FinTech focused on digital assets, in a bid to widen adoption of USD₮ and XAU₮ throughout Latin America.

The backing is intended to help Lemon create financial products built on digital assets that cost less and are simpler for customers to use.

The size of the investment was not disclosed.

The two firms initiative to extend work Lemon has already been doing to make USD₮ and XAU₮ part of everyday financial activity. To keep things straightforward for customers, Lemon provides one Digital Dollar balance underpinned by USD₮.

Sources indicate that the platform manages currencies, exchange rates and networks behind the scenes, leaving people free to concentrate on spending, saving or transferring funds. Through XAU₮, customers can also put money into gold without needing a substantial initial sum, as tokenisation allows them to hold fractional amounts of gold that can be tracked and managed within the app.

Lemon operates an app that combines digital assets with day-to-day money management. Customers can save, generate yield, buy stocks, make and receive cross-border payments and, in markets where it is offered, pay using Visa prepaid virtual cards. The firm aims to give people access to their money at any time and in any place by cutting out needless steps between users and their funds.

Neem, a provider of unified financial infrastructure for businesses in Pakistan, has secured backing from ADB Ventures as part of its Pre-Series A round to expand its presence across the country.

The size of the investment from ADB Ventures, the venture capital arm of the Asian Development Bank (ADB), was not disclosed. Neem will use the capital to grow its financial infrastructure platform and lending portfolio, improve its product capabilities and reach more of the Pakistani market.

Several other investors joined the Pre-Series A round. These include DNI Group, HI2 Global, AKD Securities Limited, Epic Angels and the Pakistan Startup Fund. Strategic angel investors from PayNet, Aspire, Stripe and other international FinTech and payments companies also took part.

According to recent reports, neem’s lending offering includes earned wage access. This lets employees draw on wages they have already earned, with a particular focus on blue-collar workers in industries that employ large workforces. The service aims to give workers a responsible option and reduce their dependence on informal borrowing. The tech giant also intends to offer financing to businesses. Merchants using its platform would be able to obtain working capital based on their transaction and settlement records, rather than only on conventional financial statements.

In a recent development, neem’s platform brings together the tools businesses need to handle the flow of money. Clients can collect payments, send out funds, oversee balances, automate settlements and reconcile transactions in one place. The company works with more than 70 enterprise customers in sectors including logistics, utilities, insurance, manufacturing and retail.

It has been revealed that the fresh funding marks the start of Neem’s next growth phase. The firm plans to extend its digital financial rails to help businesses and the broader Pakistani economy continue to digitise.

MetaDecomp: Adaptive Task Decomposition via Meta-Learned Procedural Memory

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (224 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.33822v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: Reusing past experience in long-horizon tasks requires more than storing successful procedures: Language agents must distinguish which procedures apply and what work remains as execution progresses. We introduce MetaDecomp, an in-context meta-learning framework for adaptive task decomposition that jointly learns a task-relative state space and reusable procedures. Its outer loop builds procedural memory from successful training executions, representing task progress as abstract states and procedures between states as directed acyclic graphs of operations and dependencies. As new progress distinctions are learned, MetaDecomp revisits historical execution evidence to reassess state assignments and reorganize the procedures they support. With memory fixed at test time, the inner loop refines an initial decomposition and revises it from environmental feedback, combining applicable procedure fragments with task-specific steps missing from memory. Evaluated on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld over three seeds, MetaDecomp achieves the highest mean performance among the compared methods in four of five settings, for example, an 86.3% success rate on ALFWorld with Qwen3-4B. Fixing the initial schema or omitting historical reprojection reduces performance in component ablations. MetaDecomp also uses fewer inference tokens than ReAct and AutoRefine in all five settings. Cross-benchmark analysis identifies a low-performance area where partial coverage degrades success relative to hidden memory; high coverage improves success, while low coverage changes little. Code will be released upon acceptance.
